# AI Declaration {.unnumbered}

The use of AI in this portfolio was limited to the following:

-   Code and LaTeX debugging, particularly for unnecessarily tedious problems such as plotting issues and random syntax errors.
-   Helping to explore for verifiable sources and for different types of datasets.
-   Converting handwritten solutions to LaTeX from scans, and similarly to save time in writing out the questions for the final setup.
-   Serving as an engagement tool to clarify my own understanding and misconceptions, and to question various avenues, particularly ones with no clear answer ahead.

Main AI chatlogs can be found here: <https://gemini.google.com/app/be6ba84775cbe4e4>

# Reflective Commentary {.unnumbered}

## Learning achievements {.unnumbered}

I found the whole endeavour enjoyable. It was incredibly tedious at times, but it is the kind of tedium that feels rewarding once the work comes together. In a recent conversation with Dr Birgit, I said that creating these comprehensive bodies of work is, in a sense, an artwork, and I stand by that description. I spent a large amount of time working out how to compile the document as beautifully as possible. For example, anyone scrolling through the document will notice that I manually indented the code so that everything stays contained within the code margins, and that all figures and tables within sections are labelled using `#| fig-cap` and `#| tbl-cap`. My intention was to make the portfolio read much like a dissertation, with the same attention to detail, and to make each section self-contained, so that someone could read it, understand what is going on and learn from it in that way. Framing the work like this throughout helped me to keep a holistic view of what I wanted the project to look like. I knew from the start that I did not want to bundle together a collection of scattered pieces of work and stack them on top of each other without an overarching narrative.

Beyond the development of my own mental schema, getting immersed in the work gives a deeper understanding of, and feel for, the content. Ever since my honours year I have had the impression that everything is structured so that you get out as much as you are willing to pour in, and this portfolio has been no exception. As the work progresses you start to build a sense of confidence about how well you really know what is going on, and about what you are actually capable of. Despite how corny it may sound, at this level our aim is to show that we have mastered the subject of interest and can deploy what we know in applicable scenarios and areas of interest. The portfolio gave me a concrete way of testing that for myself.

## Methodological challenges {.unnumbered}

This approach was mostly a blessing, but it did come with some curses. It is easy to get lost in random details and in the search for answers to largely irrelevant questions. This is good for understanding in my own mental framework, but it consumes a great deal of time. It also led me to set high expectations of how much I could get done in the time available. For example, my originally submitted draft of section A was a flow through two papers where $A \Rightarrow B$, effectively a mini-dissertation. I assumed that recreating simplified versions of these papers would not take very long, but as I progressed there were more and more additions to include and nuances to explain and to understand fully myself. The draft ended up being far longer than intended, and the lesson I took from it was that expanding the scope is far easier than finishing it properly.

The most irritating part of the process was the bugs. I know this every time, yet I keep thinking it will get easier: debugging, and verifying that code works under the hood, takes up the majority of the time once a method is set up. If development is not properly staged, so that everything is confirmed to be correct at every step, it is easy to muddy the results with incorrect implementations whose effects only appear much later. This is why, for most of the tutorials, my main focus was to get the code right first and to worry about the cohesion of the project afterwards.

On top of this, tests and assignments from other courses put severe time constraints on what was actually plausible. Being honest with yourself about what is possible, and knowing when to discard certain avenues, is a valuable skill to retain, and it is one that I once again had to demonstrate here. After submitting the first draft, I realised that I could not pour that level of energy into the remaining projects, and I had to tone them down deliberately. Luckily, I am at a stage at masters level where I am comfortable with the nitty-gritty details alongside time pressure. At this point the work is mostly tedious at times rather than a source of pure confusion and stress, which is a considerable change from earlier years.

## Ethical and reproducibility considerations {.unnumbered}

The elephant in the room is the remarkable capacity that AI tools have gained in such a short time. There is always a temptation to take as many shortcuts as possible, and such a tool can very easily be misused to the point where the work produced is far removed from the capabilities of the person submitting it. With this in mind, it is incredibly important that clear and honest transparency is presented, not only in an academic setting but also in the workforce. These issues have always existed. What has changed is that the avenues for acting on them are now so accessible, and produce results with little to no effort.

The concern is also not limited to AI use. It extends to the fabrication of results and plots, to the withholding of verifiable code so that results cannot be reproduced, and to work that has been plagiarised or restated without acknowledgement. For this reason I tried to do as much as I could on my own, and to rely on AI and other online sources for debugging help, as an engagement tool to verify my own understanding of the topics, and for finding important resources, all of which is documented in the AI chatlogs referred to in the declaration. The purpose of this is to ensure that I can wholeheartedly call whatever work I produce my own: that nothing in it is blindly generated, that it is a direct consequence of my active engagement, and that the narratives are always based on factual, verifiable and non-fabricated results.

## Future areas for development {.unnumbered}

With respect to future development, I need to become comfortable with more technical but efficient ways of writing code. In many cases I have largely avoided them, even though I am familiar with how they work, because the time and effort needed to get the hang of them first tends to be hard to commit to under deadline pressure. For example, the hyperparameter tuning for the local likelihood extension was restricted to an illustration rather than a full tuning exercise, because my code was largely sequential on a computation that is embarrassingly parallelisable, as my CSC2 lecturer used to say. A similar situation arose in the wavelets extension, where I restricted the simulation to 200 replications because of computational constraints, which could have been largely overcome with parallel computing. The same applies to the many opportunities I had to vectorise parts of my code. Making these techniques a routine part of my workflow, rather than something I postpone, is the most concrete next step I can identify.

Going through the projects from start to finish took a great deal of time: fixing my shorthand remarks and half sentences, adding proper structure to all of the qmds, and making sure that overall it was a coherent body of work. It was a love-hate relationship with the work. Honestly on multiple occasion I was glued to my laptop for 4+hours straight without food or water hyperfixiating on this because I had set myself the goal of finishing a certain section before doing anything else. |
